summary: A 1970 note proposing a third-level protocol called the Logger Protocol, by four authors. Third-level protocols sit above the basic host-to-host rules and define higher-level services, in this case apparently for logging in.

plainLanguage.summary: This note proposes rules for logging in to a remote computer, built on top of the basic rules of computers talking.

questions: how do you log in to a remote arpanet host
why use ascii for teletype communication
subtitle: A third-level protocol defining how users log in to and interact with remote hosts over the network

tldr.problem: The NCP protocol handles machine-to-machine connections, but there is no standard way for a user at one site to log in to a foreign host and interact with its monitor (operating system).
tldr.mechanism: Four programs at each host handle login: send-logger and receive-logger coordinate the connection, then send/receive programs handle teletype communication. Users connect to socket zero at the destination, establishing a full-duplex link that mimics a local teletype. The protocol standardizes on ASCII codes and defines break character handling.
tldr.outcome: This protocol establishes conventions that enable interactive remote login on the ARPANET, an early precursor to later protocols like Telnet.

today: RFC 56 laid out the conceptual framework for interactive remote login on the ARPANET. While the specific protocol evolved, its core principles—using reserved login sockets, establishing bidirectional connections, and standardizing character codes—influenced later login protocols including Telnet (RFC 854).

sections.title: Four-Program Design
sections.content: The Logger Protocol envisions four special programs at each host, arranged in two pairs. At the initiating site, a send-logger program accepts the user's login request. At the destination site, a receive-logger listens to socket zero (the standard login socket) and accepts incoming login attempts. After accepting, both loggers coordinate to establish a full-duplex connection between the user and the destination host's monitor. Once the connection is established, send and receive programs take over: the send program takes input from the user's teletype and transmits it down the established link, while the receive program gets output from the monitor and displays it to the user. The loggers then step out of the picture, allowing direct user-to-monitor interaction.
sections.plainLanguage: Two special programs (loggers) at each end set up the connection, and then hand off to two other programs (sender and receiver) that just pass messages back and forth between the user and the remote computer.

sections.title: Establishing the Connection
sections.content: The send-logger reserves two pairs of unused sockets and starts by connecting to socket zero at the foreign host (the receive-logger). The receive-logger checks if it has capacity and either accepts (then immediately closes the initial connection) or rejects. If accepted, the receive-logger picks its own socket pair and connects back to the send-logger. When the send-logger's socket is answered, it accepts that connection and initiates a second connection to complete the full-duplex link. Once both directions are connected, the loggers activate the send and receive programs and drop out, leaving the user in direct communication with the foreign monitor. This complex handshake ensures both sides are ready before the user connection is established.
sections.plainLanguage: The send-logger says "let me in," the receive-logger says "okay," they set up two-way communication, and then they step aside so the user can talk to the monitor.

sections.title: ASCII Standard and Break Handling
sections.content: The RFC proposes that all teletype-to-foreign-monitor communication use 128-character USASCII, the same code used by the IMPs. This simplifies character conversion: most network hosts already use ASCII or can easily translate to it. For hosts using different internal codes, the sender and receiver programs perform the translation. The protocol also addresses the critical issue of the break character, which serves two purposes: as a panic button (immediate exit from any program) and as an exit command (orderly exit from a subsystem). The panic button function can be implemented via the INT command. The proposal allows users to map seldom-used characters to these functions, accommodating different local conventions while maintaining network compatibility.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone uses the same alphabet code (ASCII) so computers can talk to each other easily. Users can pick special keys to mean "stop everything" or "exit this program."

sections.title: Transmission Modes and Buffering
sections.content: The protocol allows flexibility in how commands are grouped and sent: one mode sends several command lines as a single message, another sends a message after each carriage return, and a third sends character-by-character for interactive languages. Users can switch between modes as needed. The sender program can format these different transmission styles into a form acceptable to the remote monitor, and the receiver must buffer incoming data from different transmission modes appropriately. The RFC emphasizes that echoing should be done locally (by the user's own host) with the foreign monitor suppressing its echoes, reducing network load and improving responsiveness.
sections.plainLanguage: Users can choose whether to send messages one at a time, after each command, or character-by-character, and the protocol handles them all. Echo (showing what you typed) happens on your own computer, not the remote one.
